analysis.one_liner: Diverts part of Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts managed by private firms.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee: after referral to three committees and then to the Ways and Means Social Security Subcommittee, it received no markup and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers born in 1950 or later redirect a share of their Social Security payroll taxes — 5% of wages up to about $10,000, rising to 10% after 2015, plus an extra percentage on wages above that — into personal investment accounts. Workers would give up traditional Social Security benefits on those earnings and instead draw on their account, converted at retirement into a lifetime annuity. The bill promised a floor: if an account could not buy an annuity paying at least 150% of the poverty line, or match what traditional Social Security would have paid, the Social Security trust fund would make up the difference. It also created tax-free treatment for the accounts, a new Board and annuity agency to run the system, and budget rules capping the growth of entitlement spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Private asset managers, recordkeepers, custodians, and insurers would gain a guaranteed new stream of retirement money to manage, since the bill required the Board to contract with professional asset managers and let certified investment companies offer Tier III options to every participating worker. Workers would own accounts that are tax-free and inheritable, and would keep a government-backed floor of income at retirement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asset managers, insurers, and account holders

how_it_helps.text: Participating workers could redirect part of their payroll contributions into personal accounts, with the option to move balances above a $25,000 threshold into private investment options offered by certified firms.
Account balances, annuity payments, and qualified distributions would be exempt from federal income tax, and nothing from the accounts would count in a worker's taxable estate.

The bill guaranteed every participant at retirement either an annuity paying at least 150% of the federal poverty line or the benefit traditional Social Security would have paid, with the trust fund covering any shortfall.
Account balances would be inheritable: on a participant's death, undistributed amounts go to designated beneficiaries or the estate.
The bill dedicated budget surpluses to Social Security and imposed caps on the growth of entitlement spending, which supporters presented as shoring up the program's finances.

analysis.who_pays: Participating workers would bear market risk on their retirement savings and lose the traditional Social Security benefit earned on the redirected wages, including most disability and survivor protections tied to those earnings; administrative fees would come out of account balances. The government would finance the transition by borrowing through a new Self-Liquidating Social Security Transition Fund and by general fund transfers, and the trust fund would owe guaranteed top-up payments to every retiree whose account underperformed.

drawbacks.text: Participants lose traditional Social Security benefits on all redirected earnings, and the bill strips entitlement to old-age benefits for participants, preserving only limited child, widow, widower, parent, and survivor benefits for those who die before buying an annuity.

Retirement income would depend on investment returns; the guarantee backstop is paid from the same Social Security trust fund, so a broad market downturn late in a worker's career would push the cost onto the program rather than the worker's account.
Administrative expenses for asset managers, recordkeepers, and custodians are deducted from account earnings, eroding balances relative to Social Security's own very low administrative cost.

Diverting payroll contributions while current benefits are still owed would create a financing gap covered by a new Transition Fund borrowing and general fund transfers, adding to federal debt during the decades-long switch.
Separate provisions would cap the growth of entitlement programs, which could force cuts in other safety-net programs to help cover the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters' case rested on ownership: tax-free, inheritable accounts with a guaranteed income floor. The honest objection is that the guarantee doesn't remove risk, it relocates it — a worker whose account does poorly relies on future Congresses honoring trust-fund top-up payments, while administrative fees skim returns that Social Security's own system doesn't charge. The transition also had to be paid for with borrowing and spending caps, and the chief structural winner was the money-management industry, which would have gained a mandatory stream of fees on retirement money that previously cost almost nothing to administer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means, Budget, and Rules Committees on introduction, then a month later sent to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Paul Ryan introduced the bill on April 21, 2005, with 13 Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Budget, and Rules the day it was introduced.
On May 9, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security of Ways and Means, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security was left untouched, and the money-management industry did not get the new mandatory fee stream it would have gained. The bill's sponsor later built on the framework in subsequent Congresses, but this bill died quietly rather than being debated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traditional Social Security; asset managers got nothing

for.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 13 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Made partially privatizing Social Security the top domestic priority of his 2005 agenda, campaigning nationally for personal accounts and giving the idea momentum in the House.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup of the bill; it stayed in the Social Security Subcommittee after its May 2005 referral.

against.name: House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 2005 personal-accounts push as a bloc, denying the White House the bipartisan cover it sought and making the bill politically unusable in an election-sensitive year.

against.name: AARP
against.what_they_did: Ran a major advertising campaign against Social Security privatization in 2005, shaping public opinion against personal accounts.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the broader 2005 fight over Social Security personal accounts split almost entirely by party, with Republicans pushing privatization and Democrats opposing it.

industries.note: The bill would have routed a mandatory slice of every participating worker's payroll tax into accounts managed by contracted asset managers and, above $25,000, into options sold by certified investment companies, with fees deducted from account earnings. The industry's gain exists only because the cheaper public alternative — Social Security, which costs a fraction of a percent to administer — is diverted away for those earnings.

The bill required the Board to contract professional recordkeepers and custodians for the Tier I and Tier II funds and for annuity reserves, with their expenses paid out of account earnings. Roughly a hundred million workers' accounts would have been new recurring business.

Tier I and fixed-income accounts could be invested partly in insurance contracts, a new institutional buyer. But retirement annuities themselves would be issued by a new government Annuity Issuance Authority rather than private insurers, capping the upside.
